title: Why Do Wheels Spin Backwards on Camera?
description:
The car races forward but its wheels turn the wrong way, or freeze. Nothing is wrong with the wheel or the camera: the trick happens between the frames.
Here is the simple rule behind it, the speed at which a car wheel freezes on film, and why your own eyes can be fooled too.

Chapters
0:00 Wheels that turn the wrong way
0:35 What a camera records
1:23 The spoke that went backwards
2:30 The rule: aliasing
3:30 A real car at 35 km/h
4:25 Shutter speed
5:10 Your own eyes
6:20 The answer

Sources
- Purves, Paydarfar & Andrews (1996), The wagon wheel illusion in movies and reality, PNAS 93(8)
- Kline, Holcombe & Eagleman (2004), Illusory motion reversal is caused by rivalry, not by perceptual snapshots of the visual field, Vision Research 44
- Finlay & Dodwell (1987), Speed of apparent motion and the wagon-wheel effect, Perception & Psychophysics 41
- Schouten (1967), Subjective stroboscopy and a model of visual movement detectors
- Wikipedia: Wagon-wheel effect; Stroboscopic effect

subtitles: Why do wheels spin backwards on camera?
A car speeds up on screen.
Its wheels turn faster, then slow down, then stop.
Then they turn the wrong way, while the car keeps racing forward.
Helicopter blades can hang frozen in mid-air while the helicopter flies.
Nothing is wrong with the wheel, or with the camera.
The trick is in what happens between the pictures.
And by the end, you will see why your own eyes, in the right light, can be fooled the same way.
Start with what a camera actually records.
It does not record motion.
It records still pictures, one after another.
Cinema film shows 24 of them every second.
Most video records 25, 30, or 60.
Between two pictures, the camera sees little or nothing.
Whatever happens in that gap, it simply misses.
Your brain fills the gap.
It joins each picture to the next by guessing the shortest, simplest movement between them.
Psychologists call this apparent motion.
It is the reason a flip book, or a film, looks alive at all.
Usually that guess is right.
With a wheel, it can go badly wrong.
Here is a wagon wheel with 12 spokes.
Every spoke looks exactly like every other.
Mark one of them in gold, just for us.
The camera, and your brain, cannot see the mark.
Spin the wheel slowly.
Between two frames it turns only a few degrees.
Each spoke moves a little, and your brain matches each one with itself.
Forward.
Correct.
Now spin it faster.
Between frames, each spoke now travels almost to where the next spoke was.
Your brain does not know which spoke is which.
It sees a spoke just behind where one used to be.
So it picks the shortest move: a small step backwards.
The gold spoke went forward.
The wheel you see went back.
Spin it a little faster still, so each spoke lands exactly where its neighbour was.
Every frame now looks identical to the one before.
The wheel, turning at full speed, appears to stand perfectly still.
So the rule is simple.
What matters is how far the wheel turns between two frames.
Compare that with the gap between two spokes.
Ignore whole gaps; only the leftover counts.
Less than half a gap left over, and the wheel looks like it goes forward.
More than half a gap left over, and the nearest match is behind, so it looks like it runs backwards.
Exactly one whole gap, and it freezes.
For our 12-spoke wheel at 24 frames a second, the gap between spokes is 30 degrees.
Turn it two full times every second, and it freezes.
Engineers call this aliasing.
A fast pattern, sampled too slowly, pretends to be a slower one.
To capture a repeating motion honestly, you need more than two samples per repeat.
Fewer than that, and the samples lie.
Let's try a real car.
Take a wheel with 5 spokes and a tyre about 65 centimetres tall.
Film it at 24 frames a second.
That wheel looks frozen when each spoke moves exactly one gap per frame.
Work it out, and that happens at about 35 km/h.
A little slower, and the wheel seems to creep backwards.
A little faster, and it crawls forward.
Speed up more, and the whole cycle repeats.
Forward, frozen, backwards, again and again.
And the speed you see on screen has almost nothing to do with the real speed.
A car at highway speed can show wheels creeping slowly backwards.
The same thing freezes helicopter rotors when their blades line up with the frames.
There is one more piece.
Each frame is not an instant.
The shutter stays open for a short time, and anything moving during that time smears.
A slow shutter blurs the spokes into a soft disc, and the illusion fades.
A fast shutter freezes each spoke crisply, and the illusion gets stronger.
So footage with very short exposures shows it most clearly.
Many phone clips in bright sun are like that.
Next time you film a fan, a bike, or a car with your phone, watch the wheels.
Change the frame rate in your camera settings, and you can watch the wheel change direction.
But here is the strange part.
People have seen wheels reverse with their own eyes, with no camera at all.
Some lights do the camera's job for it.
Older fluorescent tubes and some cheap LED lamps flicker 100 or 120 times a second.
That is too fast to notice.
Under them, a spinning wheel or a machine part is lit in flashes, just like frames.
It can look slow, frozen, or reversed.
In factories this is a real danger.
A lathe that looks stopped may be spinning at full speed.
Old record turntables used this on purpose.
A ring of dots on the platter looks still under mains lighting when the speed is exactly right.
And stranger still, a few experiments report brief reversals even under steady, continuous light.
Some researchers think this means our vision takes snapshots of its own.
Others think it is a contest between motion detectors in the brain.
That question is still open.
So, why do wheels spin backwards on camera?
Because a camera sees in frames.
When each spoke's leftover step is more than halfway to the next spoke, your brain matches it to the wrong one.
The wheel goes forward.
The pictures go backwards.
Have you ever caught a wheel or a fan doing this?
Tell me where in the comments.
